entities.name: Al-Azhar Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Al-Azhar Mosque is one of the oldest mosques in Cairo and the founding structure of Al-Azhar University, built by the Fatimid general Jawhar al-Siqilli in 970-972 CE to serve as the first congregational mosque of the new Fatimid capital of Cairo. The mosque and the university that grew around it became inseparable: Al-Azhar is simultaneously a mosque where Friday prayers are held and the world's oldest continuously operating Islamic university.

Built in the Fatimid Ismaili tradition initially dedicated to the Prophet's daughter Fatima al-Zahra (from whom it takes its name), the mosque was transformed after Saladin conquered Egypt in 1171 CE and abolished the Fatimid caliphate. Al-Azhar was converted to Sunni Shafi'i practice and gradually developed into the supreme scholarly institution of Sunni Islam. Multiple minarets from different dynasties — Fatimid, Mamluk, and Ottoman — create a layered architectural record of Cairo's history.

The mosque's interior features a forest of marble columns, gold Quranic inscriptions, and ancient wooden screens from the Fatimid period. The Mamluk sultan Qansuh al-Ghawri's gate tower (1468-96 CE) and the mosque's five minarets — each from a different period — make Al-Azhar's exterior one of Cairo's most complex architectural assemblages. The mosque hosts Friday prayers attended by thousands, Quran recitation competitions, and serves as the ceremonial venue for major Islamic events announced by Al-Azhar's Grand Sheikh.
